observations.text: SP performed the fix-to-fix problem to the level required for this stage; however, the transition heading was derived only after the IP directed the sequence of the solution, and each recalculation during the transition followed an IP prompt. Arrival at the target fix was achieved with a distance error of 5 DME before the IP corrected the heading. Marginal performance for the Training Section - independent building of the point-to-point picture is expected to improve on the following sorties.

SP, working from the standardized point-to-point procedure of the Techniques and Procedures Manual, took the transition heading without the IP having to direct the solution. The heading was recalculated during the transition after two verbal prompts from the IP, and the target fix was reached with a distance error of 4 DME. Deviations were recognized and corrected, although with delay. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP established the transition heading in time and continued to refine it during the transition without IP intervention. Minor errors in the initial mental picture produced a distance error of 3 DME, which the SP recognized and corrected in a timely manner. The target fix was reached on the assigned radial with no assistance required. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP solved the fix-to-fix problem on the HSI accurately and quickly, taking the transition heading immediately after the clearance. The heading was recalculated continuously as the radial and DME relationship changed, holding the distance error inside 1 DME throughout the transition. No IP intervention or prompting was required. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP applied the standardized point-to-point solution flawlessly, taking the transition heading without hesitation and cross-checking the raw VOR/DME picture against the RNAV direct-to indication. Corrections during the transition were anticipatory, and the deviation at the target fix remained negligible, inside 1 DME and within 1 radial. Knowledge of the procedure and speed of the mental solution were above the levels desired for this stage. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP, due to a non-standardized method of building the fix-to-fix picture, did not plot the present position and the target fix against the same reference on the HSI and took a heading toward the bearing of the fix instead of the computed transition heading. The error was not corrected during the transition, with the result that the distance error exceeded 6 DME and the IP had to direct the recalculation and fly part of the transition. Further study of the point-to-point procedure in the Techniques and Procedures Manual is required.

SP, due to poor workload distribution, with navigation, communication and aircraft control attempted simultaneously, did not calculate the transition heading in the time available and did not take it before passing the initial fix. No recalculation was made during the transition, with the result that the aircraft passed abeam the target fix by more than 5 DME and the IP directed the correction and completed the intercept. Shedding of secondary tasks while the point-to-point solution is being worked requires attention.

SP solved the point-to-point problem within the standards of the Training Section; however, the transition heading was taken late and was corrected only after the IP's verbal prompts on two occasions. The distance error at the target fix reached 4 DME, at the limit of the allowable deviation, and was recognized with delay. Marginal performance - speed in assessing the transition heading is expected to improve over the next instrument sorties.

SP took the transition heading in time and recalculated it during the transition without IP prompting. Small errors in the initial estimate of the wind correction produced a distance error of 3 DME, recognized and corrected in a timely manner without the IP's intervention. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP assessed the transition heading quickly and accurately according to the standardized procedure and took it immediately on passing the initial fix. Continuous recalculation during the transition kept the distance error inside 2 DME, and the target fix was reached without any IP intervention. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP solved the fix-to-fix problem without error and cross-checked the TACAN raw data against the GPS direct-to presentation before committing to the transition heading. Deviations during the transition were negligible, with the distance error held inside 1 DME and the arrival on the target fix within 1 radial. Accuracy and speed exceeded the levels desired for this stage. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP, due to incorrect scaling of the mental picture close to the station, treated equal radial spacing as equal distance and derived a transition heading that placed the aircraft on the opposite side of the target fix. The error was not identified during the transition, with the result that the distance error passed 6 DME and the IP had to take the aircraft to re-establish the fix-to-fix geometry. The relationship between radial spacing and distance requires review before the next instrument sortie.

SP, due to over-reliance on automation that was not fully understood, accepted the RNAV direct-to steering without an independent check of the parameters and did not verify the selected waypoint against the clearance. The transition was flown toward the wrong fix and the error went undetected by the SP, with the result that the aircraft was more than 8 DME from the assigned fix when the IP intervened and re-entered the correct point. An independent raw-data cross-check of every direct-to entry is required.

SP, due to a single-shot solution of the fix-to-fix problem, took an initial transition heading but did not recalculate it as the radial and DME relationship changed during the transition. The uncorrected drift was recognized only after the IP's verbal prompts, with the result that the distance error reached 4 DME at the limit of the allowable deviation before the correction was applied.

SP, due to distraction by radio traffic during the transition, allowed the instrument cross-check to lapse and did not correct the deviation from the computed heading in time. The error was recognized and corrected with delay, after two verbal prompts from the IP, with the result that the aircraft reached the target fix with a distance error of 4 DME. Protection of the cross-check while working the radio requires attention.

SP solved the point-to-point problem within the desired standards, taking the transition heading in time and correcting without IP intervention. However, the recalculation during the transition was applied twice in large steps rather than continuously, and the distance error reached 3 DME before it was reduced. Marginal performance for the Training Section - a smoother and more continuous refinement of the transition heading is expected to improve.

SP knew and applied the standardized point-to-point solution without error, taking the transition heading immediately and refining it continuously as the geometry changed. The distance error was held inside 2 DME throughout, and the target fix was reached accurately and quickly without any IP intervention. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP built the fix-to-fix picture on the HSI before the clearance was complete and took the transition heading with no hesitation, cross-checking VOR/DME raw data against the RNAV presentation. Corrections were anticipatory rather than reactive, leaving negligible deviations, with the distance error inside 1 DME and the arrival within 1 radial of the assigned fix. Knowledge of the procedure was flawless and the mental solution was faster than required at this stage. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP, due to insufficient knowledge of the standardized fix-to-fix procedure, could not determine the transition heading from the present radial and DME pair without assistance and took no heading toward the target fix after passing the initial fix. The IP had to direct the solution step by step and fly part of the transition, with the result that the distance error at the target fix exceeded 7 DME. Further study of the point-to-point procedure in the Techniques and Procedures Manual and AFMAN 11-202 VOL3 is required.

SP, due to task saturation on the first fix-to-fix problem after the holding entry, did not work the transition heading and did not request a repeat of the assigned fix that had not been understood. No transition heading was taken and no correction was attempted, with the result that the aircraft continued outbound and the IP directed the recovery of the geometry and completed the transition. Earlier inquiry toward the IP when the clearance is not understood is required.

SP, due to a late start of the point-to-point solution, took the transition heading well after passing the initial fix and applied no wind correction to the computed track. The resulting drift was recognized only on the IP's verbal prompt, with the result that the distance error reached 4 DME at the limit of the allowable deviation before the heading was corrected. The correction was then applied correctly, but with delay.

SP, due to an aircraft state that had diverged from the SP's mental picture without being reassessed, continued on the original transition heading after the DME readout had already contradicted the expected closure. The error went undetected until the IP prompted a recheck of the radial and DME pair, with the result that the deviation from the target fix reached 4 DME and was corrected with delay. Re-establishment of the cross-check after each heading change requires attention.

SP, due to a coarse estimate of the wind correction applied to the transition heading, allowed the computed track to drift during the second half of the transition. The deviation was recognized without IP intervention and corrected in a timely manner, with the result that the distance error remained at 3 DME and was reduced before reaching the target fix.

SP, due to complacency on a problem flown repeatedly on previous sorties, relaxed the continuous recalculation of the transition heading and refined it only once during the transition. The deviation was identified by the SP and corrected without the IP's intervention, with the result that the distance error reached 3 DME on the assigned radial before being brought back. Consistent recalculation throughout the transition is expected on all point-to-point problems.

SP solved the point-to-point problem accurately and quickly, taking the transition heading in time and correcting the deviations without IP intervention. However, the accuracy was at the edge of the desired standard, with the distance error twice reaching 2 DME before the correction took effect, and the initial solution required a second look at the HSI on each problem. Marginal performance for the Training Section - a more immediate assessment of the transition heading is expected to improve.

SP knew and solved the fix-to-fix problem flawlessly, taking the transition heading without hesitation and recalculating it continuously as the radial and DME relationship changed. The raw VOR/DME picture was cross-checked against the GPS direct-to indication on every problem, and the deviations remained negligible, inside 1 DME and within 1 radial of the assigned fix. Accuracy and speed were above the levels desired for this stage of training. Above end of block MIF achieved.
